title: Count Inversions
description: Count how many pairs are out of order using a modified merge sort, and see why O(n log n) is possible.

data.text: An inversion is a pair of indices `(i, j)` with `i < j` but `nums[i] > nums[j]`. Count the number of inversions in the array. The count can be large, so return a `long`.

**Input:** `nums = [2, 4, 1, 3, 5]`

**Output:** `3`

**Explanation:** The inverted pairs are `(2,1)`, `(4,1)`, and `(4,3)`. A sorted array has zero inversions — the count measures 'how unsorted' an array is.
Check every pair with `i < j`, which is O(n²) and unusable for arrays of realistic size.

data.title: Brute force O(n²)

data.text: Merge sort already compares elements from the two halves as it merges. When the element from the right half is smaller than the element from the left half, it is smaller than **every remaining element in the left half** — and each of those forms an inversion. Counting them in bulk during the merge is what turns O(n²) into O(n log n).

data.title: Merge sort with inversion counting — O(n log n)
data.content: Count the whole remaining left half each time the right element wins.

data.title: Why the count is mid - iLeft + 1
data.text: The left half `[iLeft..mid]` is already sorted, so if `buffer[iRight]` is smaller than `buffer[iLeft]` it is also smaller than every element from `iLeft` to `mid`. Counting all of them at once avoids the inner loop entirely.

data.title: Use <= for the left-win case to stay stable
data.text: Writing `buffer[iLeft] <= buffer[iRight]` keeps equal elements from the left half first, which preserves stability and avoids double-counting equal values as inversions. Using `<` here changes the answer for arrays with duplicates.

data.caption: Each merge counts all inversions that cross the midpoint, so every pair is counted exactly once.

data.title: Complete solution
data.content: The inversion count is a real metric, not just an exercise: it quantifies how far a dataset is from sorted order, which is used in recommendation ranking and in measuring how 'surprising' a stream of values is. Counting pairs during a divide-and-conquer merge is the general technique behind many 'count pairs with property X' problems.
